title: Nitrogen Deficiency in Plants: Signs, Causes and How to Fix It
metaTitle: Nitrogen Deficiency in Plants: Signs and Fixes
metaDescription: Nitrogen deficiency shows on the old leaves first. See the signs crop by crop, what causes it, and the fertilizer sold here that fixes it.
excerpt: Nitrogen deficiency in plants starts on the old, lower leaves. Nitrogen is part of chlorophyll, the green color that lets leaves turn sunlight into food. It is also part of every amino acid and protein, so it drives leaf growth, tillers and the size of the harvest. In rice it adds tillers, panicles and filled grains, and it raises the protein in the grain. Here are the signs in each crop, what brings it, how to be sure and the fertilizer that fixes it.

heroImage.alt: Chili plants with pale yellow green leaves, older ones yellowing first, from nitrogen shortage

blocks.text: Nitrogen moves easily inside the plant, so a hungry plant pulls it out of its old leaves to feed the new ones. That is why the yellowing starts on the lower, older leaves, often at the tips, while the top leaves stay greener.
Nitrogen deficiency symptoms

The whole plant turns pale green to yellowish green and grows short and thin. The lower leaves yellow first, from the tip back, and dry up when the shortage is bad. In corn the yellow runs down the midrib of old leaves in a V shape. While rice leaves stand narrow and upright with few tillers. Flowering drops, grain and fruit stay small, and some crops ripen early with a lower yield.
Nitrogen deficiency by crop

Each crop shows it its own way. So find yours in the tables below, then open its page for the photo and the full fix, like the one for [nitrogen in rice](/nutrient-deficiencies/rice-nutrient-deficiency#nitrogen).

blocks.text: What causes nitrogen deficiency

Sandy soils and soils low in organic matter hold little nitrogen, and heavy rain or a typhoon washes nitrate below the roots. In flooded rice fields nitrogen also escapes as gas. Urea left on the surface of alkaline or calcareous soil loses ammonia to the air. Many fields simply get too little urea, or get it at the wrong time or in the wrong way. Hot weather and poorly drained, acid sulfate or saline soils also cut the supply.
How to be sure it is nitrogen

Sulfur shortage gives the same pale color, but it starts on the young leaves while nitrogen starts on the old ones. A mild iron shortage can also look like it, but iron shows first on the newest leaf as it comes out. In rice, read the top fully opened leaf of 10 plants on the PhilRice leaf color chart every week, from 14 days after transplanting. A BSWM Soil Test Kit or a DA Regional Soils Laboratory measures soil nitrogen. A leaf tissue test shows what the plant took up. Vegetable growers can also test the sap of leaf stems with nitrate test strips.
How to fix nitrogen deficiency

Topdress urea (46 0 0) or ammonium sulfate (21 0 0), or use 14 14 14. Add compost or manure for the long run. In rice, a typical PhilRice rate is 1 bag of urea per hectare in the wet season and 1.5 bags in the dry season. Apply it when more than 5 of 10 leaves read below 4 on the leaf color chart (below 3 in wet seeded rice).

A 2 percent urea spray, about 20 grams per liter of water, every two weeks is a typical rate for vegetables. Spray late in the afternoon or on a cloudy day so the leaves do not burn, and keep the soil dose going.

How to keep nitrogen deficiency away

Split nitrogen into several doses timed to growth, and keep straw, compost and legumes in the field to build organic matter. Let a soil test set the season total, and in rice let the weekly leaf color chart reading decide each topdress.

blocks.title: Too much is a problem too
blocks.text: Too much nitrogen makes extra leaves and tillers that delay heading and harvest. The soft, lush growth also draws more pests and diseases.

blocks.text: Nitrogen deficiency questions

items.q: What does nitrogen deficiency look like?
items.a: The plant turns pale or yellowish green and stays short and thin. The yellowing starts on the oldest, lowest leaves, often at the tips, while the new leaves stay greener.

items.q: What is the best fertilizer for nitrogen deficiency?
items.a: Urea (46 0 0) carries the most nitrogen per bag and is the usual topdress. Ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) suits soils that also lack sulfur, and a complete 14 14 14 adds phosphorus and potassium too.

items.q: Can I spray urea on the leaves?
items.a: Yes. A 2 percent urea spray, about 20 grams per liter of water, every two weeks is a typical rate for vegetables. Spray late in the afternoon or on a cloudy day so the leaves do not burn, and keep the soil dose.

items.q: How do I know when my rice needs more urea?
items.a: Use the PhilRice leaf color chart on the top fully opened leaf of 10 plants, every week from 14 days after transplanting. If more than 5 of the 10 leaves read below 4, it is time to topdress.
